title: Select an existing R session
summary: Connect the extension to the workspace you are already using.
images: feature-select-session.png
The native session picker lists the running R console. The example session uses R 4.5.1.
body:
## What this does
The extension attaches to an existing R console session. Your objects and retained trial results stay in that session. DataRaft does not start an R process on your behalf.

## Try it
1. Start an R console in Positron and load your DataRaft workspace.
2. Install `dataraft.ide` in the R environment used by that session.
3. Open the Command Palette and choose **DataRaft: Select R Session**.
4. Select the session whose workspace contains your products.
5. Use **DataRaft: Refresh Metadata** to populate the DataRaft views.

## Read the screenshot
The picker identifies the existing R session. Selecting it establishes the execution context for subsequent explicit commands. The R session identifier is temporary and will be different in your own workspace.

## Keep in mind
Live R commands require Positron and a trusted workspace. In a remote workspace, the extension and R must run on the same host and share access to the temporary directory. Switching sessions invalidates responses still in flight. A busy session rejects execution requests; wait until it is ready before trying again.

title: Browse the workspace overview
summary: Find products and see quality and run counts before opening details.
images: feature-overview.png
The workspace overview lists three synthetic products with individual Inspect product actions.
body:
## What this does
The overview gathers product definitions, warning or failed quality checks and recent run counts from the current metadata snapshot. Each product has an **Inspect product** action.

## Try it
1. Select an R session and choose **Refresh Metadata**.
2. Run **Open Data Product Overview**.
3. Select **Inspect product** on the product you want to understand.

## Read the screenshot
The synthetic workspace contains three product definitions. Counts describe the current metadata snapshot and may change after a trial and another refresh.

## Keep in mind
The overview does not run products. Refresh is explicit, and the summary shows only the bounded records returned by the bridge.

title: Explore a data product
summary: Read product identity, rules, columns and available actions in a guided view.
images: feature-inspect-product.png
The Positron product dashboard shows identity, contract, ports and quality rules for passing.orders.
body:
## What this does
The **Data Products** tree and **Open Data Product Overview** make workspace definitions discoverable. Inspect opens a structured dashboard with identity, governance, contract, input and output ports, columns, quality rules and sources. Available actions include trial, bounded row view, lineage and refresh.

## Try it
1. Select an R session and choose **Refresh Metadata**.
2. Open **Open Data Product Overview** or select a product in **Data Products**.
3. Read the product dashboard, then choose an explicit action when needed.

## Read the screenshot
`passing.orders` is a synthetic product with one quality rule. It has no declared contract or ports. The dashboard distinguishes a missing contract from a successful schema check.

## Keep in mind
Inspection transfers bounded metadata, never table cells. Refresh is manual. A definition's existence does not imply successful checks or publication.

title: Review contracts, policies and delivery timing
command: Select a governed product in Data Products
summary: Inspect policy definitions, output ports and SLA in one dashboard.
images: feature-product-guarantees.png
The governed.orders dashboard shows its contract columns, warehouse output port and 08:00 UTC delivery timing.
body:
## What this does
The product dashboard renders bounded lifecycle, contract, policy, port and SLA metadata as readable sections. You can see the delivery agreement without opening raw JSON.

## Try it
1. Refresh a workspace that contains a product with a contract or ports.
2. Select the product in **Data Products**.
3. Review **Contract**, **Columns**, **Policy checks**, **Input ports** and **Output ports**.

## Read the screenshot
`governed.orders` is a synthetic definition with a two-column contract and one output port named `warehouse`. Its SLA declares availability by 08:00 UTC. The preview shows the guarantee definition, not proof that the target was published on time.

## Keep in mind
The bridge omits destination paths, credentials and row values. A listed policy is a definition, not a pass decision. A declared SLA or contract is a promise to check in your workflow, not evidence of a successful release.

title: Run a product without publishing
summary: Compare successful and blocked deliveries using retained trial results.
images: feature-trial-completed.png
The successful trial has a completed badge in the native Positron product dashboard.
feature-trial-blocked.png
The failing trial has a blocked badge and its retained quality evidence can be inspected separately.
body:
## What this does
**Trial Product** explicitly executes a product through the R bridge. It retains a result that you can inspect afterwards. Configured framework destinations are not published by this command.

## Try it
1. Select the product definition, rather than a previous result.
2. Run **DataRaft: Trial Product**.
3. Read the status badge and product detail in the trial dashboard.
4. Refresh metadata, then inspect **Quality** and **Runs**.

## Compare the two screenshots
The first delivery completes its trial. The second contains a negative amount that fails the `nonnegative` rule, so its result is blocked. Both outcomes are retained as evidence. A successful bridge request can therefore contain a blocked product result: read the result status, not just whether the command finished.

These fixtures deliberately have no explicit schema contract. `completed` describes execution; schema evidence can still be `unvalidated`.

## Keep in mind
A trial still reads sources and executes your transformations and checks. User functions can have side effects of their own. Cancellation or a timeout stops the extension waiting; it does not guarantee that R code already dispatched has stopped. The bridge retains up to 20 trial results in the session.

title: Inspect failed quality evidence
command: Quality view: select a rule result
summary: See which rule failed and how many rows were affected.
images: feature-quality-evidence.png
The nonnegative rule failed for one of the two rows in failing.orders.
body:
## What this does
The **Quality** view exposes evidence retained by previous execution. Selecting a rule result opens a readable detail panel, including the affected asset, rule identifier, status and available counts.

## Try it
1. Run a trial and refresh metadata.
2. Expand **Quality** in the DataRaft view.
3. Select a failed rule for the product you want to investigate.
4. Inspect the evidence before changing the delivery or the rule.

## Read the screenshot
The selected result belongs to `failing.orders`. It reports `rule: nonnegative`, `status: failed`, `n_failed: 1` and `n_total: 2`. The **Runs** view distinguishes the completed and blocked trials. The **Incidents** view records the observed failed check.

## Keep in mind
Counts are metadata, not a preview of rejected rows. Use R-side diagnostics when you need retained row-level evidence. An incident here describes an observed failed or unchecked check; it does not represent a complete incident-management or resolution workflow.

title: Locate a failed rule in R code
summary: Map a retained failure to a verified location in your R source.
images: rule-diagnostic.png
The failed nonnegative function rule is marked in its original workspace R file.
body:
## What this does
After a trial, DataRaft can map a failed function rule back to a verified R source location. This command uses the retained result and does not rerun the product.

## Try it
1. Define the rule in an R file and load it using `source(..., keep.source = TRUE)`.
2. Run the product trial.
3. Select its retained result and choose **Show R Rule Diagnostics**.
4. Open the indicated file or inspect the Problems view.

## Read the screenshot
The native editor displays the source-reference diagnostic for the `nonnegative` rule. The location comes from the real R function's source reference. The message identifies the rule and its failed status without transferring failure rows or raw condition text.

## Keep in mind
Ordinary formula rules do not provide supported source locations. The file must be unchanged, UTF-8, within the workspace and within the size limit. Dirty or stale buffers receive no marker. Markers clear on edits, refresh and session/context changes. No marker does not mean the rule passed; the command reports omitted locations separately.

title: View bounded rows inside R
command: DataRaft: View Bounded Rows in R
summary: Open a small data preview in the native Data Explorer.
images: bounded-data-explorer.png
The Data Explorer shows exactly three rows from a retained result containing twenty rows.
body:
## What this does
The explicit **View Bounded Rows in R** command opens a bounded existing table or retained tabular result in Positron's native R Data Explorer. The extension receives an acknowledgement, not the table cells.

## Try it
1. Select a viewable table or retained successful result.
2. Run **View Bounded Rows in R**.
3. Inspect the native Data Explorer's columns and row count.
4. Configure `dataraft.maximumRows` if a different preview limit is appropriate.

## Read the screenshot
The capture uses `dataraft.maximumRows = 3` and shows three rows and two columns. The underlying successful result has twenty rows. This is a bounded view, not evidence that all rows were inspected visually.

## Keep in mind
The default preview limit is 100 rows and the maximum is 1,000. Model manifests and results without retained viewable output are not supported by this command. Data remains in the R viewer, but anyone with access to that viewer can see the selected rows.

title: Follow directed product lineage
host: Positron; offline lineage metadata is also supported
summary: Inspect dependencies and jump from a graph node to its product.
images: feature-directed-lineage.png
The native lineage panel shows the current workspace dependency metadata.
body:
## What this does
The lineage panel represents directed relationships from metadata. Nodes support keyboard focus. Selecting a product node reveals the matching product in the Data Products tree.

## Try it
1. Refresh the workspace or connected lake metadata.
2. Run **Show Directed Lineage**.
3. Follow the directed relationships between sources and products.
4. Select a product node to locate the matching tree item.

## Read the screenshot
This is the real lineage panel for the synthetic acceptance-test workspace. The graph is a snapshot, with a generation timestamp. It is not a live animation of a running pipeline. The native test also verifies that selecting `passing.orders` reveals its corresponding product in the tree.

## Keep in mind
Refresh is explicit. The bridge limits metadata collections, and offline lineage snapshots accept at most 500 nodes and 500 edges. The graph describes the relationships present in the supplied metadata; it does not infer every dependency hidden inside arbitrary user code.

title: Edit an ODCS contract
summary: Work with contract fields while keeping YAML as the authoritative document.
images: feature-yaml-editor.png
The production custom editor displays fields from native.contract.yaml.
body:
## What this does
The custom editor helps you edit an ODCS 3.2 YAML contract. Fields are grouped by identity, schema and quality, and the underlying YAML is available in a collapsible panel. It preserves comments and unknown metadata. The YAML document remains the source of truth.

## Try it
1. Open a saved ODCS contract YAML file.
2. Choose **DataRaft: Open Contract YAML Editor**.
3. Edit a field, or use the controls for columns and quality rules.
4. Choose **Preview field edits** before applying anything.

## Read the screenshot
The form belongs to the actual `native.contract.yaml` file in the synthetic workspace. The screenshot is captured in Positron; the same offline YAML editor is available in VS Code without a live R session.

## Keep in mind
Editing a contract document does not validate a full dataset. The portable `dr_contract_yaml()` metadata export is not an executable ODCS contract. R-based validation and bounded sampling are separate explicit commands and require Positron.

title: Review a proposed YAML change
command: Preview field edits → review diff → apply or discard
summary: Inspect the actual proposed diff before changing the document.
images: feature-yaml-diff.png
The native diff viewer compares the proposed contract change with the current document.
feature-yaml-preview.png
The editor offers explicit Apply preview to document and Discard preview controls.
body:
## What this does
Preview creates a proposed edit and opens the native diff viewer. The document itself remains unchanged until you explicitly apply the preview.

## Try it
1. Change a contract field.
2. Select **Preview field edits**.
3. Inspect the proposed diff, including any formatting or metadata changes.
4. Return to the contract editor and choose **Apply preview to document** or **Discard preview**.

## Read the screenshots
The diff proposes changing the synthetic contract name to `Applied form change`. The separate preview screenshot shows the discard decision from another edit. The acceptance test verifies that preview alone leaves both the document and the saved file unchanged.

## Keep in mind
The proposal is tied to a specific document version. A concurrent text edit invalidates it. Review the current state and create a new preview instead of applying a stale proposal.

title: Apply a change, then save explicitly
summary: Keep the distinction between an editor change and a saved contract.
images: feature-yaml-applied.png
The applied form value is visible and the contract tab has an unsaved-change indicator.
body:
## What this does
Applying an accepted preview makes a version-checked workspace edit. The document is left unsaved so you can still review, undo or save it using the normal editor workflow.

## Try it
1. Review a proposed change in the diff viewer.
2. Choose **Apply preview to document**.
3. Check the changed field and the unsaved marker on the tab.
4. Save the YAML explicitly when you are ready.

## Read the screenshot
The form now contains `Applied form change`. The dirty-document indicator distinguishes this state from a persisted contract. In the native test, the saved file still matches its baseline immediately after Apply.

## Keep in mind
**Validate Saved ODCS Contract in R** reads the saved file, not an unsaved form proposal. If another program changes the file, preserve your work, review the external changes, then close and reopen the contract editor to establish a fresh saved-file baseline.
